activity.notes: In 1136, after the death of Jutta of Sponheim, the Benedictine women's community at Disibodenberg selected Hildegard to succeed her as magistra. Around 1150 Hildegard founded her own women's monastery at Rupertsberg near Bingen, and in 1165 established a second house at Eibingen; Vatican sources describe her as abbess of both houses. Her religious leadership was inseparable from a major body of visionary theology, preaching, sacred music, correspondence, natural philosophy, and medical writing, but these overlapping activities do not represent distinct political relationships and are therefore not split into parallel ATLAS Activities. She died at Rupertsberg on 17 September 1179. The stable polity binding is the Holy Roman Empire, encompassing her activity across Disibodenberg and Bingen rather than forcing a narrower local ecclesiastical territory across her change of monastic seat.

sources.title: Apostolic Letter proclaiming Hildegard of Bingen as a Doctor of the Church
sources.citation_text: The Vatican records Hildegard's succession to Jutta as magistra around 1136, her foundation of Rupertsberg around 1150 and a second monastery in 1165, describes her as abbess of both, and gives her death at Rupertsberg on 17 September 1179.

sources.title: General Audience of 1 September 2010: Saint Hildegard of Bingen
sources.citation_text: The Vatican states that in 1136 the sisters chose Hildegard to succeed Jutta as leader of the Benedictine women's community and describes her competence in both spiritual and organizational leadership.

sources.title: Hildegard von Bingen: Life and Work
sources.citation_text: The City of Bingen's Museum am Strom identifies Hildegard as abbess, visionary, theologian, composer and healer and documents Rupertsberg in Bingen as her historic workplace.

sources.title: Heilige Hildegard von Bingen
sources.citation_text: The Mainz Cathedral Museum states that Hildegard led the Benedictine women's community at Disibodenberg from 1136, founded her own monastery at Rupertsberg in 1147, and established a daughter house at Eibingen in 1165, while emphasizing the scope of her theological writings.
